summary.title: Little Lisp interpreter
summary.one_liner: You learn how a small Lisp interpreter works by walking through its tokenizer, parser, scope-chained execution context, and lambda evaluation in about 116 lines of JavaScript.
keywords: build a lisp interpreter in javascript
takeaways: Lisp code is parsed in two phases: tokenize() adds spaces around parentheses and splits on whitespace, and parenthesize() builds a nested array of typed atoms.
Atoms are labelled as identifiers or literals (numbers, strings) by categorize().
An execution context is a chain of scopes; identifier lookup checks the current scope and then walks up to the enclosing scope.
Lambdas are represented as JavaScript functions returned by special.lambda(), which bind arguments into a new scope on invocation.
The whole interpreter is about 116 lines of JavaScript, meant to show how simple writing an interpreter can be.
summary.summary: The author walks through Little Lisp, a small Lisp interpreter written in JavaScript for a lightning talk at the Recurse Center. The article first introduces basic Lisp forms (atoms, lists, function invocations, lambdas), then explains the parser, which tokenizes the source and recursively parenthesizes it into a nested array of typed atoms. It then covers the interpreter: a Context object that chains scopes for variable lookup, and interpret/interpretList functions that evaluate special forms like lambda and invoke JavaScript functions. It closes by pointing to the GitHub repository and to Peter Norvig's lis.py as a comparison.
